sourceFieldStructure.scenarios: Each scenario = number + title (xlsx header "Name:") + one text cell (xlsx header "Scenarios:") containing three labeled parts separated by blank lines: "Situation:", "Parent Reaction:", "Teacher Goal:". xlsx header for the number column is the Excel default "Column1".
sourceFieldStructure.parentTypes: Each parent type = Name + Description only. No behaviors, sample lines, difficulty, or other fields.

parentTypes.name: The Ally
parentTypes.description: They view the teacher as a partner. They value communication, support classroom rules, and foster resilience when their child faces academic hurdles.

parentTypes.name: The Helicopter Parent
parentTypes.description: Ever-present and highly protective, they hover over every detail of their child's day. They often struggle to let the child manage tasks or make age-appropriate mistakes.

parentTypes.name: The "Know More Than You" Parent
parentTypes.description: Highly intelligent and opinionated, they regularly challenge test questions or instructional methods and may correct formatting errors in your emails.

parentTypes.name: The "It's Never My Child's Fault" Parent
parentTypes.description: Highly defensive, they quickly absolve their child of blame. If a grade is poor or a rule is broken, they will attribute the blame to the teacher or peers.

parentTypes.name: The "It's Always My Child's Fault" Parent
parentTypes.description: At the opposite end of the spectrum, they are overly critical of their child. They assume wrongdoing on their child's part before hearing the full story.

parentTypes.name: The Tiger Parent
parentTypes.description: Strict and demanding, they expect perfection. They push their children relentlessly to achieve top marks and excel in extracurriculars, creating high-pressure environments.

parentTypes.name: The Ghost Parent
parentTypes.description: MIA (Missing in Action). They rarely attend parent-teacher meetings, fail to respond to messages, and only surface if a massive behavioral or academic crisis occurs.

parentTypes.name: The Overhead Parent
parentTypes.description: They jump to conclusions and have a problem with something in the classroom, but skip communicating directly with the teacher—going straight to the principal or superintendent instead.

parentTypes.name: The Hurried/Indifferent Parent
parentTypes.description: Unenthusiastic about school events, they view parent-teacher meetings as a chore. They make minimal appearances and show low overall communication.

parentTypes.name: The Fellow Educator Parent
parentTypes.description: They have friends in education, are former governors, or were once educators themselves. They often offer unsolicited advice on pedagogy and frequently reference out-of-date teaching philosophies.
